cells: PREDICTION NUDGES  |  IA type → provisional prediction → WHY? → revisit maths
Show only nudge choices relevant to statistics or modelling AND the student's data context; do not display the whole library.
After a student selects a suitable prediction, ask WHY they expect it, then: 'If true, what would that mean for [selected beneficiary]?' Provide an inline 'Edit who this is for?' control.

Use the current answer to 'Who is it for?' (self / audience / both) from Planning. On edits, refresh the implication prompt and request confirmation of any previously typed answer; never erase it automatically.
Offer a free-text prediction and 'Not sure yet'. Contradictory results are valid; do not reward guessing a strong relationship.
For no-data/theoretical ideas, offer a conjecture and teacher check-in without requiring datasets or statistical predictions.
Do you expect a roughly linear positive relationship?
Scatter plots and Pearson's r; Linear regression

Planning only: this is a tentative prediction for PAIRED numerical data. After the real scatter, decide whether PMCC adds value; discuss linearity/outliers/causation when actually calculating/interpreting it.
Do you expect a roughly linear negative relationship?
Scatter plots and Pearson's r; Linear regression
Planning only: a negative relation is one possibility, not an observed result. Check the ACTUAL scatter first; interpret correlation and method-specific limitations only if subsequently used.
Could the relationship be curved rather than straight?
Spearman's rank correlation; Compare and evaluate fitted models
Linear, quadratic or polynomial functions; explore scatter plot
Planning only: predicted curvature is not evidence. If the actual plot is monotonic but curved, a course-appropriate rank/model technique MAY suit; discuss the mathematics at actual use.
Might there be little or no clear relationship?
Sampling and descriptive statistics; Scatter plots and Pearson's r
Sampling and descriptive statistics; Pearson's correlation coefficient
A weak/absent relationship is a valid possible finding, not a failure. Wait for actual paired observations before deciding whether any coefficient would help the aim.
Do you predict an approximately symmetric, bell-shaped distribution?
Sampling and descriptive statistics; Normal distribution
Sampling and descriptive statistics; Normal distribution
A normal model is a possible future approach only after inspecting real continuous numerical data. Explain fit and its restrictions with the ACTUAL model, not the prediction.
Do you expect a skewed distribution or outliers?
Compare median, spread and outliers; do not assume normality.
Do you expect distinct clusters or more than one peak?
Investigate whether the data mix subgroups before using one normal curve.
Do you expect one group to have a higher mean than another?
Sampling and descriptive statistics; Two-sample t-test
Two-sample t-test is in the AI SL menu, not AA SL. This is a possible planning idea only; discuss assumptions and limitations WHEN performing a justified test.
Might the groups differ more in spread than in mean?
A comparison of means is not a test of spread; use appropriate measures.
Do you predict an association between these categories?
Chi-squared test for independence; Conditional probability or expected value
Conditional probability and expected value; descriptive frequencies
Chi-squared independence is an AI SL menu option; it is not mandatory merely because categories exist. Evaluate expected counts/assumptions if the test is later ACTUALLY performed.
No association is an informative possible finding, not a failure.
Do you expect the count of successes to follow a binomial distribution?
A binomial model may be suitable with fixed trials, two outcomes, stable probability and independence; evaluate these conditions WHEN using the real model, not as a collection-stage critique.
Do you predict a roughly constant rate of change, giving a linear model?
Linear functions and models; Linear regression
Linear, quadratic or polynomial functions; Linear regression
PMCC is only a potential technique for ACTUAL paired numerical data that look approximately linear. Model-fit limitations are discussed when a model is actually fitted.
Do you predict a roughly fixed percentage increase or decrease per period?
Exponential growth or decay; Geometric sequences and series
Exponential or logarithmic functions; Arithmetic or geometric sequences
Constant percentage change differs from a constant absolute change.
Do you expect a maximum, minimum or change of direction?
Quadratic or cubic models; Optimisation using differentiation
Linear, quadratic or polynomial functions; Stationary points and optimisation
A predicted turning point doesn't demonstrate a quadratic law. Introduce genuine constraints with the model and assess the real optimum/domain once mathematical work is performed.
Do you predict a pattern repeating at regular intervals?
Check that enough cycles exist and periodicity is plausible.
Might one quantity change approximately as a power of another?
Power models; Compare and evaluate fitted models
Logarithms and exponential relationships; functions comparisons
Fit and interpretation matter; outside-course methods need teacher discussion.
Do you expect there to be a best value, such as a maximum capacity or minimum cost?
Optimisation using differentiation; Area, surface area and volume models
Stationary points and optimisation; Definite integration and areas
Optimisation needs a clear objective, relevant constraints and a realistic model.
Could more than one model be needed to describe the situation?
Compare functions and check model behaviour
A weak fit can prompt useful model comparison and reflection.
Do you have a tentative conjecture about a mathematical pattern or property?
Do not force data-based predictions on a theoretical investigation.
I have a different prediction and would like to describe it.
Do not invent a method from ambiguous free text; offer teacher guidance.
Not sure yet — I would like to examine an initial sample or simplified example.
Existing selections; exploratory maths as appropriate
Existing selections; exploratory maths as appropriate
No penalty for uncertainty; encourage a safe concrete first action.
